card ms-store  [decided]
One append-only pipeline log holds every step's start, end, and cost
why: The metrics and the debugging trace come from the same facts: when each step started and ended, what it cost, and how it ended. One event log with one fold serves both, in the same shape as the decision log and the board log.
subtree: 4 cards, 3 open, 1 decided

**The pipeline log.** One append-only file for the whole project, one event per line, in the shape of the decision log (#pr-log).
- A step started, and a step ended, for every step of every stage: a plan turn, spec, tickets, each builder pass, each check, the grader, each reviewer, a merge, the held-out set.
- An ended event carries the wall time, the cost and token breakdown (#ms-cost), the result, and for a red step its gate and cause (#ms-fail).
- Every metric is a pure fold over this log. No metric is stored as a summary that can disagree with the events.

**Detail outside the log.** Agent transcripts and full check output are files beside the log (#ms-store-files).

**Git.** What is committed and what is not: #ms-store-git.

**What stays where it is.** The board log keeps only where a ticket is and what happened to it (#vi-board-state). It does not hold step events.

  -> refines         ms-self  Measure the pipeline's cost, failures and escapes, to choose how to change the pipeline
  -> depends_on      ms-cost  Each stage records its cost in dollars and wall time, at the finest grain it can attribute
       why: An ended event carries the cost fields that this card defines.
  <- alternative_to  ms-store:opt0  Step events go into the board log
  <- alternative_to  ms-store:opt1  One directory per build, each with its own event file and its transcripts
  <- alternative_to  ms-store:opt2  A summary record per pass, written beside the transcripts and not committed
  <- refines         ms-store-plan  A plan turn's cost is written to the pipeline log when the turn ends
  <- refines         ms-store-files  Agent transcripts and check output are files beside the pipeline log, named by its events
  <- refines         ms-store-git  Git tracks the pipeline log, not the transcripts and check output
  <- depends_on      werk-cli-fails  `werk fails` reports the builder loop's failed passes by gate and cause
  <- depends_on      vi-flow-localrate  The Measure tab shows the share of one-card diagram redraws that stayed local
  <- depends_on      vi-measure  Measure is a fifth tab for the pipeline and tool measures, beside Flow
  <- depends_on      ms-fail  Each failed pass records which gate failed it, and the cause
Options
  ms-store:opt0  Step events go into the board log
    why not: The board is folded on every render, and step events outnumber ticket moves about tenfold. It also mixes build churn into the record of where a ticket is, the same reason the board is separate from the decision log.
  ms-store:opt1  One directory per build, each with its own event file and its transcripts
    why not: Debugging one build is easier, but every report has to read every directory, and a plan turn belongs to no build. A filter on the build id in one log gives the same view of one build.
  ms-store:opt2  A summary record per pass, written beside the transcripts and not committed
    why not: The summary repeats what the board log already says about a pass, so the two can disagree. It has no step-level start and end for debugging, and it is lost with the worktree.
card ms-store-plan  [open]
A plan turn's cost is written to the pipeline log when the turn ends
why: Claude Code deletes old session transcripts, after 30 days by default. A plan cost that is read back from transcripts later is lost for every turn older than that.

- The chat pane receives each turn's cost and token use when the turn ends. It appends one step-ended event for the turn at that moment.
- The event names the conversation and the card that was open on that turn (#ms-cost).
- A turn that runs while no card is open name

A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts. Chat-pane questions are not stops; they are measured on their own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

- **Kinds of stop.** A gate that waits for a person to pass it. A ticket held in blocked by a failed check, held as stuck, held because a cited card changed, or blocked with no check. A merge loop that stopped. A merge that was red on the main line, or that conflicted with it. A build that reached its retry cap.
- **Where the kind comes from.** The structured facts the build writes with each stop: the gate events, the check that holds a blocked ticket, how the merge loop ended, the merge result and its conflict flag, and the build's end at the cap. The reason text never decides the kind, so rewording a reason changes no row. A move written before those facts existed has only its reason, and for that move alone the start of the reason decides the kind.
- **Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. A red merge lasts until the ticket moves on from building. The log does not say who acted, so the panel reports the length of the stop, not a person's response time. A stop still open counts up to now and is drawn as a ring.
- **Marks.** One dot per stop, one row per kind, at the length of the wait on a log axis, because a stop lasts minutes or days. The median of the current window per row.
- **Outlier.** A dot above its row's band is amber, and a dot above 1.5 times the band's top is red. A row with too few stops says how many more it needs.
- **Drill-down.** A dot opens the ticket, run or gate where the build stopped, with the reason the log holds.

The kinds in the image are an earlier set. The marks, the band and the median follow the image.

![Waits per kind of stop, coloured against the band](/api/image?name=vi-flow-ms-waits.png)

       why: The rows are the kinds of stop and the wait time that this card defines.

  -> refines         vi-measure  Measure is a fifth tab for the pipeline and tool measures, beside Flow

  <- alternative_to  vi-flow-ms-waits:opt1  Structured facts only, with no fallback for older moves
  <- depends_on      vi-flow-ms-stage-unit  The stage panel switches its unit between dollars, tokens and wall time

    why not: A reason is prose for a person. A reworded reason drops its stops from the panel, and three kinds of blocked ticket read as one.

card st-plan-extend  [decided]
A plan over a subtree extends that subtree's spec and open tickets, and a run is not an entity
why: A second or interrupted plan over the same subtree otherwise puts a second, full ticket set on the board beside the first.
subtree: 3 cards, 3 decided

A plan over a subtree first looks for the spec and the tickets that an earlier plan wrote for the same subtree. When they exist, the plan extends them. It updates the one spec of the subtree (#st-spec) and changes the open tickets in place, under their own ids. It does not write a second set.

Open means ready or blocked. A ticket in building, merging or done stays as it is, because only the merge loop moves it (#werk-board-control). The new and changed tickets cover only the scope that those tickets do not already cover.

Planning produces a spec and tickets, and nothing else. There is no run entity that owns them (the same rejection as #st-run-issue).

A plan over a parent or a child of an earlier plan's subtree is an overlap. This card does not settle the overlap case.

  -> refines         st-spec  Plan ends with one spec per subtree, then tickets from the spec
  -> depends_on      werk-board-control  A person reorders, archives, and triggers the build of one ticket at a time
       why: It leaves building, merging and done tickets alone because #werk-board-control lets only the merge loop move them.
  -> depends_on      st-run-issue  A run is one pass at one issue
       why: It drops the run entity for the reason #st-run-issue already gives against inventing one.
  -> depends_on      st-ticket-shape  Every ticket shares one fixed structure: five header lines, then three sections in a fixed order
       why: It changes tickets in place, so it relies on the fixed ticket structure that this card defines.
  <- alternative_to  st-plan-extend:opt0  Each plan writes a new run with its own spec and a full ticket set
  <- refines         st-plan-main  Tickets merge straight onto the main line, with no integration branch
  <- refines         st-plan-archive  A plan archives an open ticket that the subtree's current spec no longer needs
  <- depends_on      werk-cli-build  `werk target`, `werk plan`, `werk loop`, `werk build`, `werk run`, `werk gate` and `werk ticket` start the build stages
  <- depends_on      st-ticket-watch  A change to a cited card blocks every open ticket that cites it
  <- depends_on      vi-board-plan  A plan is a persistent card below the board columns, colored by its state, linked from its tickets and from its subtree in the map
  <- depends_on      werk-board-build-subtree  One press on a decided map card plans its subtree and then runs the merge loop, with no pause between
Options
  st-plan-extend:opt0  Each plan writes a new run with its own spec and a full ticket set
    why not: A second or interrupted plan over the same subtree puts a duplicate ticket set on the board, and the person has to find it and archive it.
card st-spec-linked  [decided]
The plan scope is the subtree plus every decided card it depends on, followed down and never up
why: A decision two links away, under a card the subtree links, reached the planner only as a title, and the planner filled the gap itself. Following every dependency, and every card below it, hands the planner each decision the subtree rests on. Stopping at parents and at undecided or postponed cards keeps the scope to what the subtree needs.

The plan stage reads every card in the scope in full. The scope starts with the subtree. Then, until nothing new comes in, each card in the scope adds every card it depends on, together with that card's own subtree. The walk never goes from a card to its parent, because the way up leads to the whole map.

Only decided cards are in the scope. The walk stops at an open, proto, stale or postponed card and does not go below it. To keep a feature out of a build, postpone it.

card ms-cost-history  [decided]
Past plan cost is rebuilt from the agent transcripts that past sessions left on disk
why: Plan ran for a month before cost recording existed. The transcripts already hold every response's token counts, model and time, so the base for plan cost need not wait 30 more days.

- **Source.** Each past session left a transcript. Each model response in it carries input, output, cache-read and cache-write tokens, the model, and a timestamp. A response split into several blocks repeats its counts: count each response once. A subagent's transcript counts toward the turn that started it.
- **Storage.** The backfill reads the transcripts once and appends one plan-turn event per finished turn to the pipeline log, the same event a live turn writes (see #ms-store-plan). Every report folds the log and never reads a transcript, because Claude Code deletes old transcripts. A turn already in the log is skipped, so the backfill can run again at any time. The last turn of a session written to in the last 15 minutes may not be finished, so it waits for a later run.
- **Facts, not shares.** The event holds the turn's facts: its open card, the cards it wrote, how many responses wrote to the map and how many changed code, the cost, tokens and wall time. The counting rule below runs in the fold, so a change to the rule needs no rewrite of the log.
- **Dollars.** Tokens times the price for that model and token kind. A cache write is priced by its lifetime (5 minutes or 1 hour). Fast mode costs twice the standard rate. Each event names the date its price table is valid from. A session on a subscription did not pay these prices, so the result is an API-equivalent cost, not a bill. A response from a model with no price counts as zero and is reported.
- **Wall time.** From the person's message to the last response of that turn. A gap of more than 15 minutes between two responses is idle: a background task woke the turn again. Idle time is not wall time. A turn counts in the day it ended.
- **Chat-pane turns.** Each is plan cost for the card that was open in that turn (see #werk-mc-split). A session is a chat-pane session when the conversation store names it, or when its prompts name an open card. The store names only the current session of each conversation. Chat-pane turns hold about 88% of past cost.
- **Terminal turns.** A terminal turn is plan cost when it wrote to the map. Its cost is split in equal parts over the cards it wrote. A turn that only changes code is not plan cost. Terminal turns that wrote to the map hold about 9% of past cost. The other 2%

card pr-log  [decided]
The map is stored as an append-only event log, and the cards are folded from it
why: The map on screen is the fold of the whole log: the latest title, body and links of each card. A turn that rewrites a card adds an event, and the fold shows only the result.
card vi-board  [decided]
A ticket board is a view beside the map, the graph, and the diagram
why: Tickets are units of build work, not decisions. A person reads them as columns to move through, not as a tree.
subtree: 14 cards, 14 decided, 1 unchallenged

A small board in the style of Trello. One column per ticket state, one card per ticket (#st-ticket). It follows the tickets through the whole run.

On the board, a ticket card shows only its title. Clicking a card opens a drawer beneath the board: the slice (often a few hundred words, since a real ticket brief is long) sits in a main column on the left, and the metadata and relations — the map cards it cites, what blocks it, retries, files, checks (#st-ticket's fields) — sit in a sidebar on the right. A click on a cited id in the sidebar opens that card on the map. A ticket that has retried more than once shows a small retry count next to its title.

A ticket with unmet blocked_by tickets shows a small count next to its title too, one per not-done ticket it depends on — the same kind of blocking-issue count Linear shows.

A building ticket with a live agent session pulses. It stops the moment the session ends, whether that is a pass, a failed retry waiting on the next attempt, or a person stopping the build by hand — pulsing means a session is running right now, not just that the ticket sits in building.

For a ticket currently in building, the drawer also shows a live preview of the agent's log, above the slice, in a fixed-height scrolling viewport. Moving out of building — forward or back to ready — drops the preview; it is a window onto a running session, not a permanent transcript.

The columns are in #werk-board-columns. What a person can do on the board is in #werk-board-control.

  -> refines         visual  The visual artifact is the primary medium
  -> depends_on      st-ticket  A ticket is a tracer-bullet slice of decided cards
       why: The board shows the tickets, their states and fields that #st-ticket defines.

# Every task is a make target that calls the package.json script — see #lp-checks-scripts
# and #werk-devex-tasks. The rubric names the target; this file names the tool.
# `make` with no target lists the targets: each `## ` comment is the line it prints.

.DEFAULT_GOAL := help
.PHONY: help bun-version dev serve fix check test test-coverage typecheck lint e2e

BUN_WANT := $(shell cat .bun-version)

help: ## List the targets
	@grep -E '^[a-z0-9-]+:.*## ' $(MAKEFILE_LIST) | sed -E 's/:.*## /\t/' | expand -t 16

# Every target starts here. Bun ships breaking changes in minor releases (#werk-devex-toolver).
bun-version:
	@have=$$(bun --version 2>/dev/null); \
	if [ "$$have" != "$(BUN_WANT)" ]; then \
		echo "werk needs Bun $(BUN_WANT) (.bun-version), found: $${have:-none}."; \
		echo "Install it: curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash -s bun-v$(BUN_WANT)"; \
		exit 1; \
	fi

dev: bun-version ## Start werk with hot reload
	bun run dev

serve: bun-version ## Start werk without hot reload
	bun run serve

fix: bun-version ## Apply the linter's safe fixes
	bun run lint:fix

check: lint typecheck test-coverage e2e ## Run every check, fastest first

test: bun-version ## Unit tests
	CI=true bun run test

test-coverage: bun-version ## Unit tests with the coverage gate
	CI=true bun run test:coverage

typecheck: bun-version ## Type check

Follow-ups: requests after a finished build, as plan misses or build misses
why: Plan has no exit code. A request after a finished build is the clearest sign of what the plan or the build got wrong.

Each follow-up gets one of two classes:
- **Plan miss.** The build did what the plan said, and the plan was wrong or silent. Example: A must be something else. Rebuild.
- **Build miss.** The plan was right, and the build got it wrong. Example: B has a logical bug. A build miss is also an escape (#ms-outcome-escape).

**Early signals of plan misses.** These come before the person sees the build:
- each assumption the builder records where the spec was silent
- the spec-gap fails of #ms-fail

**Gate.** Each fail names its gate: a check by name, such as type check, lint or unit test (#lp-checks); the grader, with the card the diff failed against (#lp-prod-judge); a review area, with the finding's severity (#lp-prod-review); or the merge loop, for a conflict with another ticket (#st-build-run). A gate that judged nothing — a stalled or looping pass, a broken step — is named too, and has no cause.

**Cause.** Each fail gets one cause:

- *builder error*: an earlier pass got the code wrong, and the spec was clear. The gate says whether it broke a check or missed the spec, so one cause covers both.
- *test is wrong*: the test asserts old behaviour, and the diff is right. Only a check or a merge fail can have it.
- *spec gap*: the spec does not say what the diff should do.
- *false finding*: the finding passes on the next pass with no change to the code it names.
- *check infrastructure*: the check crashed, timed out, or lacked its tool, and the code did not run.
- *flaky*: the check passes on a rerun with no change to the code.
- *conflict*: the ticket clashes with work merged after it was built. Only a merge fail can have it.

#ms-fail-cause says who sets each cause.

**Derived numbers.** The first-pass success rate, the cap-hit rate (the share of builds that reach the retry cap, #st-build-ticket), the passes per build as median, 90th percentile and maximum, and the fails by cause and by gate. A build is one run of the builder loop over one ticket. A ticket that the merge loop sends back builds twice, and each build counts on its own.

**Starting thresholds.** These are guesses until data exists. Each needs a minimum sample, so that one bad build does not fire it.

- A cap-hit rate above 10%, over at least 10 builds, points at ticket size or spec quality, not at the builder.
- One gate key that fails three builds in a row becomes a check or a rubric line (#ms-rubric).
- A false-finding share above 20% for one reviewer or the grader, over at least 5 of its fails, means its prompt needs a fix.
- Any flaky or check-infrastructure fail is a fix to that check, not to the builder.

Each stop already leaves a structured fact in the board log or the pipeline log, so the count and the wait time are a fold, and only a restart needs a fact it does not leave yet." --body "A stop is a place where the build cannot go on until a person acts.

**Kinds of stop.**
- A gate that waits for a person to pass it.
- A ticket held in blocked: by a failed check, as stuck, because a cited card changed, or with no check.
- A merge loop that stopped.
- A merge that was red on the main line, or that conflicted with it.
- A build that reached its retry cap.
- A restart of unfinished work, which ends the tickets of the subtree that had not merged (#werk-board-restart).

A builder's question is not a stop: the overseer answers it, not a person. A gate has no reject: a person who does not accept the result asks for a change, and that is a follow-up (#ms-outcome-followup). A chat-pane question is measured on its own (#ms-outcome-interv-chat).

**Where the kind comes from.** The structured facts that the build writes with each stop: the gate events, the check that holds a blocked ticket, how the merge loop ended, the merge result and its conflict flag, the end of a build at the cap, and the restart flag on each ticket a restart ends. The reason text never decides the kind, so a reworded reason changes no count. A move written before those facts existed has only its reason, and for that move alone the start of the reason decides the kind.

**Length of a wait.** From the stop to the next event that moves the work on. The log does not say who acted, so the length is that of the stop, not a person's response time. A stop still open counts up to now.

**Numbers.** Stops per ticket and per card, by kind, and the total wait.

**Starting threshold.** Stops per ticket must go down over time. A rise raises an alert by the rule of #lp-trend-alert.

Example. Ticket app/02 \"Add an item\".

1. 10:00 — a check fails in building, and the ticket moves to blocked with the check named. A stop of kind blocked by a failed check starts.
2. 11:30 — the person moves it to ready. The stop ends: 1 h 30 min.
3. 12:00 — the run reaches the gate and waits. A stop of kind gate starts.
4. If the person has not passed the gate yet, the stop counts up to now.

\`\`\`
app/02   10:00 [blocked: check] ── 1h30 ── 11:30 ready     12:00 [gate] ── open ──► now
stops:   1 x blocked by a check (1h30)   1 x gate (open)
\`\`\`"

The chat pane now writes each turn's cost to the pipeline log live, as #ms-store-plan requires.

**What works now**
- The chat pane receives a turn's result, waits 2 seconds for the transcript to be complete, then appends one plan-turn event. Only the backfill (`werk cost import`) wrote these events before.
- The event is built from the turn's transcript with the same pricing as the backfill. Subagent cost counts toward the turn, and the event's time is when the turn ended. If the turn names no open card, the conversation's home card fills it.
- The turn is the last one the person started before the result came. So a queued message sent right after the result is not recorded as that turn.
- Both writers identify a turn by its session and prompt id. A live turn is written once, and a later backfill skips it.
- A failed write prints one line to stderr. It never stops the conversation.

> A background task that wakes a chat turn after its end adds cost that the record of that turn does not hold.

Explain this one first.
New session 453e2351.

A turn can start work that runs in the background and finishes after the turn ends. The finished task wakes the agent again without a new message from you. The agent then reads the result and answers, and those answers cost money. The live recorder has already written the turn by that time, so it drops that cost.

This conversation had two such wakes. The two forks finished after my turn ended, and each one woke me:

```
you: "let's go with A"          ← one prompt, one turn id
│
├─ my turn: map edits, start 2 forks ($X)
├─ result ──► +2 s: recorder writes the turn: $X      ✔ in the log
│
│   … forks run in the background …
│
├─ fork 1 done ──► wake: I read its report, run tests ($Y)
├─ result ──► recorder: "this turn id is already in the log" → skip   ✘ $Y lost
│
├─ fork 2 done ──► wake: full checks, the reply to you ($Z)
└─ result ──► skip                                                     ✘ $Z lost
```

The cause is the key. The recorder and the backfill both identify a turn by its session and prompt id. A wake has no new prompt, so it has the same key as the turn that started the task. The first record wins, and the later cost is skipped. The backfill `werk cost import` skips it too, because the key is already in the log.

The fix: write one event per result, not one per prompt. The key becomes session, prompt id and result number. Each wake then adds its own event, and the fold adds them up into the turn. Nothing is counted twice, and the backfill uses the same key.

Both fixes work. All 1056 unit tests pass, and the coverage gate passes. The type check fails only in the old errors in `src/fold.test.ts`.

**1. Wake costs are recorded.** Each result of a turn now writes its own part of the turn. A wake from a background task becomes the next part, with only the responses since the part before. The live record and `werk cost import` both key a part by session, prompt id and part number, so nothing is counted twice. The report adds the parts into one turn and counts one turn, not one per part.

Older events have no subagent count. For them, the code counts every subagent as already recorded, so the old history is not counted twice.

**2. Code rework is computed.** Run `node src/cli.ts rework`. The report on the real target repo:

```
Rework over 53 merged tickets, window 14 days
  cited cards reopened after the build started: 0
  merged lines changed in the window: 560 of 13147, in 19 tickets
  merges whose window is still open: 45
  merges the repository no longer holds the commits of: werk/01 … werk/16 (8)
```

- The report finds a ticket's commits by their subject `werk build <ticket>: pass N`, because werk merges by fast-forward. It then counts with `git blame` how many of the ticket's lines are still there at the end of the 14 days.
- I checked the 0 for reopened cards against the logs. The only reopened cited card was reopened before the tickets that cite it started to build.
- The report takes about 24 seconds, so it is a command you run, not part of every Measure read.
